passage:
"Shh, shh, Tenzin, I've got you."
Tenzin's cheeks were wet. He had bumped his head on the table and was crying hard.
"Ow," he sobbed.
"Ow, yes. That hurt." Dolma held him close and rocked side to side. "Om mani... om mani..." she hummed, low and slow.
Tenzin's crying got softer. He pressed his face into her shoulder.
"There. Breathe with me." She rubbed his back in circles.
Tenzin hiccupped. Then he lifted his head and pointed at the table. "Bad."
"Silly table," Dolma said softly. "Shall we give it a pat?"

qa.q: What did Tenzin bump his head on?
qa.a: He bumped his head on the table.

qa.q: What does Tenzin pressing his face into Dolma's shoulder suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he was starting to feel safe and calmer, since his crying also got softer as she held him.

qa.q: Which parts of Dolma's response helped soothe him?
qa.a: She held him, rocked him, hummed slowly and rubbed his back, using touch, voice and rhythm to calm him.

qa.q: What would change if Dolma had told Tenzin to stop crying at once?
qa.a: He would probably stay upset longer, because a toddler cannot calm himself yet and needs her help to settle.

grounding: It shows a toddler being calmed through a caregiver's touch, voice and rhythm.

passage:
Creche note, Written by Charu, caregiver.
Aparna (14 months) had a hard drop-off today. When her mother left she screamed and pushed away the toys. I didn't try to distract her. I picked her up, held her against my chest and walked slowly by the window, singing the same lullaby over and over. After a few minutes she stopped arching her back and her breathing slowed. She fell asleep on my shoulder.
Next: I'll use the same song at every drop-off so it becomes familiar. 🤍

qa.q: What did Charu sing while walking by the window?
qa.a: Charu sang the same lullaby over and over.

qa.q: What does Aparna's arching back and pushing away toys suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was very distressed and overwhelmed after her mother left.

qa.q: Why is Charu's plan to use the same song at every drop-off a good idea?
qa.a: A familiar song can become a reliable comfort that helps Aparna settle faster each time.

qa.q: How might Aparna's mother feel reading this note?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that her daughter was comforted with care, even if it's hard to hear she screamed.

grounding: It shows a caregiver soothing a toddler through holding, slow movement and song.

passage:
Thunder cracked over the village and the lights went out. Bhupen, two, began to wail in the dark.
Nikita lifted him onto her lap on the charpai, wrapped her shawl around them both and rocked, humming a Bihu tune and patting his back in time.
Another rumble came. Bhupen stiffened, then relaxed as she kept patting. His sobs turned into sniffs. When the rain softened, his thumb was in his mouth and his eyes were drooping.

qa.q: What did Nikita wrap around both of them?
qa.a: She wrapped her shawl around both of them.

qa.q: How can you tell Bhupen was still scared when the next rumble came?
qa.a: He stiffened at the sound, showing he was still frightened before relaxing again with her patting.

qa.q: What could a caregiver learn from Nikita's approach?
qa.a: Steady rocking, humming and patting in rhythm can calm a small child who cannot settle himself yet.

qa.q: What is it like for Nikita in the dark storm?
qa.a: She has to stay calm herself so her steady rhythm can reassure Bhupen, even though the storm is loud around them.

grounding: It shows a toddler calmed by touch, voice and rhythm in a rural home during a storm.

passage:
The winter dark came early in Malmö, and Xin, eighteen months old, woke from her nap screaming. Her face was red and her fists were tight.

Lars picked her up and held her against his chest. He walked slowly around the kitchen, patting her back in a steady rhythm and humming the same low tune. "Shh, I've got you."

Her cries turned to hiccups. Her fingers uncurled on his sweater. After a few minutes she was quiet, one cheek on his shoulder, watching the window.

qa.q: What was Lars doing as he walked around the kitchen?
qa.a: He patted Xin's back in a steady rhythm and hummed the same low tune.

qa.q: What do Xin's uncurling fingers suggest about how she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest her body was relaxing and she was beginning to feel safe and calm in Lars's arms.

qa.q: What worked well in how Lars soothed Xin?
qa.a: He used close holding, a slow steady walk, patting and a familiar tune, which a young child can lean on before she can calm herself.

qa.q: How might Lars feel as Xin quietens down?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and close to her once the crying turns to calm.

grounding: Shows a toddler abroad being calmed by a parent's touch, voice and rhythm.

passage: I'm Tarun, Vinita's uncle. Last Sunday she fell off the sofa at our house and howled. I tried talking fast and waving toys; it made things worse. Then her mother lifted her, rocked side to side, and sang the same short lullaby slowly, again and again. Her mother's hand made small circles on Vinita's back. Within a minute Vinita's crying slowed. She tucked her head under her mother's chin. I don't know exactly what changed inside her, but I noticed the slow rhythm did what my toys couldn't.

qa.q: What did Tarun try first when Vinita cried?
qa.a: He tried talking fast and waving toys, which made things worse.

qa.q: Why might Vinita have tucked her head under her mother's chin?
qa.a: She seemed to feel safe and comforted, looking for closeness as her body calmed, though Tarun cannot be sure what she felt.

qa.q: What could Tarun try next time Vinita is upset?
qa.a: He could hold her close, slow down, and use a calm voice and steady rocking instead of fast talk and toys.

qa.q: How might Vinita's mother feel when she calms her daughter?
qa.a: She would likely feel steady and connected, glad that her touch and song can settle Vinita.

grounding: An uncle observes a toddler being calmed by her mother's rocking, song and touch.

passage:
The pressure cooker in their Kolkata kitchen whistled suddenly, and eighteen-month-old Imran jumped, dropped his ball and screamed.
Dilnaz scooped him up and held him against her. “Shh, shh, it's only the cooker.” She rocked from foot to foot, patting his back, slow and steady, and sang the rhyme about the moon.
His crying turned to hiccups. His fist loosened on her kurta.
By the end of the rhyme he was pointing at the cooker, frowning, but calm.

qa.q: What made Imran jump?
qa.a: The pressure cooker whistled suddenly.

qa.q: How did Imran feel when the cooker whistled, and how did that change?
qa.a: He was frightened and screamed, but he became calm as his mother rocked and sang.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do that helped him calm down?
qa.a: She held him close, rocked, patted his back in a steady rhythm and sang a familiar rhyme.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz had just told him to stop crying from across the room?
qa.a: Without her touch and voice nearby, Imran would probably have stayed scared much longer.

grounding: A mother soothes her startled toddler with touch, rhythm and a familiar rhyme.

passage:
The power cut came on the coldest January night, just after Lohri, and baby Ritu woke crying in the dark.
“Seema, is she hungry?” Dadu called.
“No, she just ate. The fan stopped. She's scared of the quiet,” Seema-Dadi said, lifting her.
Dadi held Ritu against her shawl and swayed. She sang low, “Lori, lori, so ja.” Ritu's cries slowed. Her fingers found Dadi's earring and held it.
“She's quiet,” Dadu whispered.
“Shh. Let her sleep.”

qa.q: What did Dadi hold Ritu against?
qa.a: She held Ritu against her shawl.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she woke in the dark?
qa.a: She was frightened by the dark and the sudden quiet when the fan stopped.

qa.q: What helped Seema-Dadi calm Ritu?
qa.a: Holding her close, swaying and singing a low lullaby gave her comfort and rhythm.

qa.q: How might Dadu feel as Ritu becomes quiet?
qa.a: He is relieved and careful, whispering so as not to wake her.

grounding: A grandmother soothes a frightened baby with touch, voice and rhythm during a winter power cut.

passage:
Daycare note, Diwali week. By Jahnavi, carer.
At 4 p.m., crackers burst outside the window. Mridul, two, screamed and ran to me. I picked him up and held him close against my chest, swaying slowly. I hummed the same lullaby we sing at nap time and stroked his back in circles. His breathing slowed. After a few minutes he rested his cheek on my shoulder and sucked his thumb. We moved to the far room. I told his mother at pickup. 🤍

qa.q: What time did the crackers burst?
qa.a: At 4 p.m.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when the crackers burst?
qa.a: He was frightened and startled, screaming and running to Jahnavi.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do to soothe Mridul?
qa.a: She held him close, swayed, hummed a familiar lullaby, stroked his back and moved to a quieter room.

qa.q: How might Mridul's mother feel hearing about it?
qa.a: She would likely feel reassured that Jahnavi comforted him calmly.

grounding: A daycare carer soothes a startled toddler during Diwali crackers with touch, rhythm and a familiar song.
